_note: Composed menus (#219): each recipe's course, weight and main proteins, and a wine to match. A starter suits a main when it is lighter and shares no protein with it; a dessert suits a main when the two weights add up to no more than rich (light 0, medium 1, rich 2). Wine pairings are general guidance for the owner to review, not a sommelier's list. Recipes with no entry here count as medium mains with no wine.

wine.name: Sangiovese or Chianti
wine.why: Bright acidity and soft tannin cut through the rich tomato and beef sauce.

wine.name: Off-dry Riesling
wine.why: A little sweetness and acidity suit the soy and sesame.

wine.name: Gewürztraminer or off-dry Riesling
wine.why: Aromatic and slightly sweet, it softens the spice and the cream.

wine.name: Assyrtiko or dry Sauvignon Blanc
wine.why: Crisp and citrusy, it matches the olives, feta and vinegar.

wine.name: Dry Riesling
wine.why: Fresh and zesty, it keeps up with the ginger and oyster sauce.

wine.name: Lightly oaked Chardonnay
wine.why: Round and soft, it suits the mild, creamy almond sauce.

wine.name: Pinot Gris
wine.why: Soft and lightly spiced, it does not fight the turmeric and cumin.

wine.name: Grenache
wine.why: A fruity, low-tannin red that sits well with the warm spices.

wine.name: Off-dry Chenin Blanc
wine.why: Its fruit and acidity balance the chilli and the coconut.

wine.name: Pinot Noir
wine.why: A light red with soft tannin suits seared beef and the sharp lime dip.

wine.name: Off-dry Riesling
wine.why: A little sweetness calms the chilli and lifts the lemongrass.

wine.name: Dry Riesling
wine.why: Lime-like and crisp, it suits the fresh herbs and the dressing.

wine.name: Dry sparkling wine
wine.why: Bubbles and acidity refresh the palate between the fresh herbs and the hoisin.

wine.name: Pinot Gris or Pinot Noir
wine.why: Pork and apple like a soft white, or a light red if you prefer.
